document.abstract: Millions of videocassettes are still stored on shelves, carrying valuable content waiting to be transferred into files before decomposing. Time is running short: not only does tape stock decay, but videotape recorder (VTR) availability becomes critical, and VTR service experts are becoming rare. As it is the final transfer, a technology for highly automated large-scale and lossless transfer that recovers and retains the original signal on tape is required. Direct tape transfer is a new technology that directly converts the off-tape signal from analog videotapes into digital files without passing through conventional playback circuits and its quality-degrading multiple analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog conversions of standard video playback equipment. By digitizing the radio frequency (RF) tape signal directly, all subsequent signal processes can be done by software with a much higher resolution than any that conventional VTR allows. Intelligent signal regeneration by smart dropout prevention and digital concealment algorithms allows signal recovery far beyond the possibilities of traditional dropout compensation circuitry. The paper explains the technical details of direct tape transfer technology, which was developed in a joint research project by the Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits IIS and Cube-Tec International GmbH.

authors.bio: Jürgen Burghardt is currently a consultant for broadcast and AV/IT business development, project management, and training. He received a M.Sc. degree in electrical engineering from Ruhr Universität Bochum. — Burghardt previously worked at Sony Deutschland GmbH – Professional Solutions Europe, where he was head of broadcast marketing, broadcast strategy, and market development. He was also a lecturer for students of media-economics at the University of Applied Science in Wiesbaden. He currently lectures on “video production technologies” at University of Applied Science in Cologne. — Burghardt is a board member and project manager of FKTG, a German association for television and cinema engineers. He is also a member of the advisory board for media at Technical University in Ilmenau, Thuringia, Germany. He is author of the German Handbook of Professional Video Recorders.
authors.name: Jurgen Burghardt

authors.bio: Joerg Houpert studied electrical engineering at the University of Bremen, with a focus on digital signal processing and psychoacoustics. During his studies in 1990, he founded Houpert Digital Audio (HDA) at the Innovation and Technology Center at Bremen and worked as a visiting lecturer at the University of Oldenburg. In 2005, he established Cube-Tec International. As head of technology at CubeTec, his current interest is to pioneer new technologies for the safeguarding of the worldwide audiovisual cultural heritage and create better solutions for the management of media workflows. Houpert is a member of SMPTE.
authors.name: Jorg Houpert

authors.bio: Timo Meyer graduated from the University of Bremen in 2009 with a diploma in electrical engineering/information technology. From 2006 until 2009 he gained practical production experience in sound broadcasting at public broadcaster Radio Bremen. —After his studies, he worked as a software developer in the area of digital audio and video signal processing with a focus on quality control and restoration at Cube-Tec International GmbH. Since 2013, he has been working as a software engineer in the field of sonar signal processing.
authors.name: Timo Mayer
